roles.label: Pediatrician
roles.script_opener: I'd love your help getting the right equipment for my child so they can move, learn, and play with more freedom. Can we talk about what a referral and a Letter of Medical Necessity would look like?

roles.label: Physical Therapist (PT)
roles.script_opener: We're ready to find equipment that fits my child's body and their goals, and I'd love your expert eye on what to trial first.

roles.label: Occupational Therapist (OT)
roles.script_opener: I'd like to make everyday routines easier and more joyful for my child, and I'm hoping you can help me figure out which equipment will do that.

roles.label: Social Worker
roles.script_opener: I'm working to get equipment for my child and I'd love your help mapping out every funding path, from Medicaid to waivers to grants.

roles.label: Behavioral Therapist
roles.script_opener: I want to make sure the equipment we choose supports my child's comfort and participation, so I'd love your insights on what works for them.

roles.label: School Nurse
roles.script_opener: I'd like to partner with you so my child can use their equipment safely and comfortably all day at school.

roles.label: School Administration
roles.script_opener: I'm here to make sure my child's equipment and access needs are fully supported on campus, and I'd like to build the plan together.

roles.label: Teacher
roles.script_opener: I want my child to take part in every part of your classroom, and I'd love to talk about how their equipment fits into the day.

roles.label: Special Education Specialist
roles.script_opener: I'd like to make sure my child's equipment needs are clearly written into their plan, and I have some questions about what the school can provide or support.

roles.label: Special Needs Trust Attorney
roles.script_opener: I want to understand how equipment purchases can be paid for from a special needs trust or ABLE account without affecting my child's benefits.

equipment.name: Custom Manual Wheelchair
equipment.who_it_helps: Children and young adults who can propel themselves or be pushed and need a chair that fits their body, supports posture, and grows with them. A well-fitted chair means more independence at school, at home, and on the playground.
who_prescribes: Pediatrician with PT or OT evaluation
typical_steps: Request a referral to a seating and mobility clinic or evaluation from your pediatrician or physiatrist.
Attend the seating evaluation with the PT or OT and an assistive technology professional (ATP) to measure and discuss goals.
Trial one or more chairs in the places your child actually uses them, such as home, school, and outdoors.
Your clinician writes a Letter of Medical Necessity and the vendor submits the prior authorization.
Wait for the decision, and appeal with your clinician's help if there is a denial.
Attend the delivery and fitting appointment and make sure the chair is adjusted to your child's body.
Schedule a follow-up check within a few weeks, and again as your child grows.
lmn_must_include: Diagnosis and a plain description of functional mobility limits
Why a standard or loaner chair would not meet your child's needs
Specific features requested (frame, cushion, backrest, adjustability) with a reason for each
How the chair supports mobility-related activities of daily living at home, school, and in the community
Results of trials with other chairs
Growth and adjustability plan
Clinician's credentials and the date of the in-person evaluation

equipment.name: Power Wheelchair
equipment.who_it_helps: Children and young adults who cannot propel a manual chair efficiently or safely, or who tire quickly. Power mobility opens up independence, exploration, and social life.
typical_steps: Ask your pediatrician or physiatrist for a referral to a seating and mobility clinic with power chair experience.
Complete a seating and mobility evaluation covering driving ability, seating needs, and the home and school environment.
Trial drive power chairs, including different drive controls such as a joystick or alternative access.
Your clinician writes the Letter of Medical Necessity and the vendor submits prior authorization.
Wait for approval, and appeal with your team's help if the request is denied.
Attend the delivery and fitting, including programming and driving practice.
Follow up on driving skills, seating, and repairs after a few weeks and as your child grows.
lmn_must_include: Diagnosis and a clear description of mobility limits
Why a manual chair or scooter cannot safely meet daily mobility needs
Results of power chair trials and driving skills
Seating features such as tilt, recline, or elevating leg rests, with the reason for each
Home, school, and community access for the chair, including transportation
Safety and cognitive readiness for power mobility
Clinician credentials and the date of the in-person evaluation

equipment.name: Cane (support cane and white cane)
equipment.who_it_helps: Support canes help young people with balance or limited mobility walk with more stability. White canes help children and young adults with blindness or low vision travel safely and independently, with training from an orientation and mobility (O&M) specialist.
who_prescribes: Orientation and mobility (O&M) specialist for white canes
Teacher of students with visual impairments (TVI)
typical_steps: Ask your pediatrician, physiatrist, or eye doctor for an evaluation referral, to a PT for a support cane or to an O&M specialist for a white cane.
Complete the evaluation, including gait and balance for a support cane or travel skills and vision for a white cane.
Try several cane types, tips, and lengths, such as folding, rolling-tip, or support canes with a quad base.
Your clinician writes a letter documenting need and the vendor handles any prior authorization.
Receive and fit the cane, adjusting height and grip.
Practice with a PT or O&M specialist in the places your child actually travels, such as school and neighborhood.
Follow up as your child grows and re-fit, since cane length changes with height and skill.
lmn_must_include: Diagnosis, including vision or mobility findings
Specific functional limits, such as balance, fatigue, or travel without sight
Why the cane type, length, and tip were chosen
Trial results and safety observations
How the cane supports daily activities and independent travel
Training plan with an O&M specialist or PT
Clinician credentials and date of evaluation

equipment.name: Walker or Gait Trainer
equipment.who_it_helps: Children and young adults who can bear some weight and want to walk or practice walking with support. Gait trainers add trunk and pelvic support for children who need more help staying upright.
typical_steps: Ask your pediatrician or physiatrist for a PT evaluation and referral.
The PT assesses walking ability, strength, and goals and tries options in clinic.
Trial different walkers or gait trainers, including support options and wheel styles.
Your clinician writes a Letter of Medical Necessity and the vendor submits prior authorization.
Wait for approval, and appeal with your clinician's help if there is a denial.
Attend the delivery and fitting and learn how to adjust and use the device safely.
Follow up with the PT in a few weeks and as your child grows.
lmn_must_include: Diagnosis and current walking ability
Why a standard walker or no device is not enough
Specific supports requested, such as trunk, pelvic, or forearm supports
Trial results and safety observations
Goals for walking at home and school
Plan for use with braces or orthotics
Clinician credentials and date of evaluation

equipment.name: Stander
equipment.who_it_helps: Children and young adults who cannot stand on their own and benefit from supported standing for bone health, circulation, digestion, and joyful eye-level time with friends.
typical_steps: Ask your pediatrician or physiatrist for a PT evaluation and referral.
The PT assesses standing tolerance, posture, hip and joint health, and goals.
Trial standers in clinic, such as supine, prone, or sit-to-stand models.
Your clinician writes a Letter of Medical Necessity and the vendor submits prior authorization.
Wait for approval, and appeal with your clinician's help if there is a denial.
Attend delivery and fitting and learn safe set-up and a standing schedule.
Follow up with the PT after a few weeks and again as your child grows.

Why supported standing is needed, such as bone density, hip health, circulation, or digestion

equipment.name: Home Ramp
equipment.who_it_helps: Families who need safe, independent access to their home for a child or young adult using a wheelchair, walker, or other mobility equipment.
who_prescribes: Contractor or ramp specialist for design
typical_steps: Ask your pediatrician, OT, or PT for a home assessment referral.
The OT or PT visits to measure the entry, slope, landings, and door widths and discusses your child's equipment.
Choose a ramp type, such as modular, portable, or permanent, with your clinician and installer.
Your clinician writes a Letter of Medical Necessity or support letter, and the vendor or contractor gets quotes and submits any needed approvals.
Wait for funding decisions, and check landlord or HOA permission if you rent or live in shared housing.
Installation, followed by an inspection and a trial with your child's equipment.
Follow up if the ramp needs changes as your child's equipment or needs change.
lmn_must_include: Diagnosis and the equipment your child uses
Description of current barriers at each entrance
Why a ramp, not stairs or lifting, is the only safe option
Required slope, length, width, and landings
Safety risks to your child and caregivers without a ramp
Home assessment findings and date
Clinician credentials

equipment.name: Vehicle Ramp or Lift
equipment.who_it_helps: Families who need safe, reliable ways to get a child or young adult in a wheelchair in and out of a vehicle, whether through a ramp, lift, or modified van.
who_prescribes: Occupational Therapist or driver rehabilitation specialist
typical_steps: Ask your pediatrician or OT for an evaluation and referral to a mobility dealer experienced with children.
The OT or PT assesses transfers, wheelchair size, seating, securement, and travel needs.
Compare vehicle options, such as ramp van, lift, or add-on equipment, and try them with your child.
Get quotes and your clinician's letter, and check which funding sources apply.
Wait for approvals, noting that many insurers do not cover vehicles, and plan alternative funding.
Install and fit the equipment and test securement and travel.
Follow up on safety checks and re-adjust as your child grows or their chair changes.

equipment.name: Bath or Shower Chair

Trial different chairs, such as tub transfer benches, rolling shower chairs, or tilted commode-shower chairs.
Your clinician writes a Letter of Medical Necessity and the vendor submits prior authorization.
Wait for approval, and appeal with your clinician's help if there is a denial.
Delivery and set-up, including checking the fit in your bathroom.
Follow up on comfort and safety after a few weeks and as your child grows.

lmn_glossary.plain: The reason a doctor or therapist says your child truly needs a piece of equipment to stay healthy and function in daily life.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: Insurers approve or deny equipment based on whether it meets their definition of medical necessity.

lmn_glossary.plain: Everyday tasks like getting around the house, toileting, dressing, eating, and bathing that depend on being able to move.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: Many insurers require the letter to show equipment helps with MRADLs in the home.

lmn_glossary.plain: What your child cannot do, or cannot do safely, because of their condition, described in everyday terms.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: Specific limits like 'cannot walk 20 feet without assistance' are stronger than a diagnosis alone.

lmn_glossary.plain: A seating feature that tips the whole seat back while keeping the hips and knees at the same angle.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: It helps with posture, pressure relief, and comfort over a long day.

lmn_glossary.plain: The distance from the seat of the chair to the floor, which affects transfers, foot placement, and table height.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: The right height can make transfers, propelling, and tabletop work safer and easier.

lmn_glossary.plain: Parts that let a chair or device be lengthened or widened as your child grows.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: A letter that requests growth features can save money and delay the need for a replacement.

lmn_glossary.plain: Insurance approval you must get before the equipment is ordered or delivered.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: Equipment ordered without prior authorization may not be covered.

lmn_glossary.plain: A standard billing code that identifies each type of equipment or supply.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: The code on the order must match what the letter describes, or the claim can be denied.

lmn_glossary.plain: A chance to try equipment at home or school before it is ordered or approved.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: Trial results are strong evidence that a specific item meets your child's needs.

lmn_glossary.plain: Reusable medical equipment such as wheelchairs, walkers, standers, and bath chairs.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: DME is the category insurance uses, and it comes with specific rules and supplier requirements.

lmn_glossary.plain: An insurer's practice of approving the cheapest option that they think will work.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: Your letter should explain why cheaper options will not meet your child's needs.

lmn_glossary.plain: The chance of skin damage from sitting or lying in one position too long.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: Showing pressure risk can support features like tilt and special cushions.

lmn_glossary.plain: A visit by a therapist to check how equipment will work in your actual home.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: Insurers often want proof that the equipment fits your doors, hallways, and bathroom.

lmn_glossary.plain: A denial is when insurance says no. An appeal is your right to ask them to reconsider.
lmn_glossary.why_it_matters: Many denials are overturned with stronger letters, trial results, and persistence.
